items.title: On-demand injection always runs the current code
items.body:
**Key: pages opened before an extension update always get current code.**

With content scripts declared in the manifest, Chrome injects them when a page loads. After the extension updates, tabs that were already open keep no working content script until they reload, so clicks fail. With on-demand injection, the popup pings the tab and, if nothing answers, injects `contentScript.js` right then, from the currently installed version. The improvement plan names this as the side benefit.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The service worker no longer wakes*: the service worker only stamps an install time either way.
- *Autofill runs automatically*: every action is still started by a click in the popup.
- *Content scripts read cross-origin iframes*: injection mode does not change cross-origin rules.

excerpts.quote: Side benefit: this also fixes the "extension updated but old pages have no content script" failure mode — injection always ships the current code.
await chrome.scripting.executeScript({ target: { tabId }, files: ["contentScript.js"] });

items.title: Start here: a careful job-application autofill extension
items.body:
"eli apply mate" is a Chrome extension (Manifest V3) that fills standard job-application fields (name, email, education, yes/no questions) after you click a button. Its promise is caution: no network calls, no auto-submit, and it only fills a field when it is confident.

The `fable` folder reviews it in three files:

1. `fable/01-codebase-overview.md`: the data flow from popup click to content script, and a module map. Read the status note at the top first: the docs describe v0.1.0, the code is v0.2.0.
2. `fable/02-findings.md`: ten findings ordered by severity. Each has the v0.1.0 bug, a suggested fix, and a dated **Status** line saying what v0.2.0 changed. Most quizzes come from here.
3. `fable/03-improvements.md`: the prioritized improvement plan.

For each finding, read the old code quoted in the guide, then open the v0.2.0 file and line in the Status note and compare.

excerpts.quote: `eli apply mate` is a Manifest V3 Chrome extension that autofills high-confidence, standardized job-application fields after an explicit click.
Line numbers in each finding refer to v0.1.0. The dated **Status** lines cite the v0.2.0 code in this snapshot.

readMore.why: The data-flow diagram from the popup to the content script modules.

items.title: Reading a finding: bug, fix, status
items.body:
Each finding in `02-findings.md` has the same parts: a severity, the file and line in v0.1.0, an explanation (often with a concrete failing input), a **Fix**, and a **Status** line for v0.2.0: Fixed, Mostly fixed, Addressed, or Open.

Two habits make these easier:

- **Find the concrete input.** Most findings name one (a profile with a particular skill, a label like "Email address", two unnamed radio groups). Trace it through the old code yourself, then through the new code, and write down exactly what the user would see.
- **Read the Status line critically.** For "Mostly fixed" and "Open", work out which inputs still misbehave in v0.2.0; those cases are worth a test of your own.

For every finding, also write one sentence on *why* it is a problem worth filing, even when the visible behaviour looks fine today. Severity follows from what the harm is and how often it happens.

excerpts.quote: **Severity: High (crash)** · `src/shared/profileSchema.ts:15-16`, `src/shared/fieldMatchers.ts:256-259`

items.title: A window flag stops the content script registering twice
items.body:
**Key: a second injection adds a duplicate listener and module state.**

With on-demand injection, the popup may inject `contentScript.js` into a tab where it is already running (for example after the ping fails for some other reason). Running the file again would call `initContentScript()` again, adding a second message listener and a second copy of the script's state, so one click could be handled twice. The first injection sets `window.__eliApplyMateLoaded = true`; later injections see the flag and skip initialization.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Signals the site's scripts*: the flag is for the extension's own guard.
- *Persists across reloads*: a `window` property disappears when the page reloads.
- *Chrome refuses to run a file twice*: Chrome will run it again, which is exactly why the guard is needed.

excerpts.quote: // The popup injects this script on demand; guard against running twice in one page.
if (!window.__eliApplyMateLoaded) { window.__eliApplyMateLoaded = true; initContentScript(); }

items.title: ShowLastResult with no result: mappings computed, then thrown away
items.body:
**Key: neither Detect nor Autofill ran, so the result lists stayed empty.**

In v0.1.0, when `ShowLastResult` arrived and `lastResult` was null, the handler fell through to the normal path: it scanned and mapped the page. But filling the `filled`, `skipped` and `unsure` lists only happens for `Detect` or `Autofill` requests. This request was neither, so all lists stayed empty and the sidebar showed zeros, even though fields had just been detected. v0.2.0 returns "Nothing to show yet. Run Autofill or Detect first." instead.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Reset to zeros on navigation*: `lastResult` was simply null; nothing reset it.
- *The renderer never got the fields*: the problem was the empty lists, not the hand-off.
- *No fillable fields*: the guide says fields existed and were detected.

excerpts.quote: but since the request type is neither `Detect` nor `Autofill`, `filled`/`skipped`/`unsure` all stay empty.
if (!lastResult) { return { ok: false, error: "Nothing to show yet. Run Autofill or Detect first." };

items.title: Free-text yes/no questions are review-only in v0.2.0
items.body:
**Key: as medium and review-only, as no option list means no yes/no.**

A free-text input has no options to choose from. v0.1.0's `hasRecognizedYesNo` returned true for any bare input, so it typed a literal "Yes" with high confidence. In v0.2.0, `hasRecognizedYesNo` returns `false` when the field has no options, and the callers fall back to *medium*. Medium is not written by `shouldFill`, so the field appears in the sidebar for the user to review. A test named "downgrades bare text inputs to review-only instead of typing Yes" pins it.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Skipped and recorded as unrecognized*: it is classified as medium, not skipped.
- *Fills the saved sentence*: the matcher produces a yes/no value, not free text from the profile.
- *"Yes" with high confidence*: that was the v0.1.0 bug.

excerpts.quote: // Typing a literal "Yes"/"No" into a free-text control is risky, so bare // inputs and textareas are never treated as a clear yes/no set; they fall // back to medium (review-only) in the callers. if (!field.options || field.options.length === 0) return false;

items.title: Correct only by accident of check order
items.body:
**Key: only the undocumented order of checks protected it.**

The location pattern `\b(location|city|address)\b` does match "Email address". Email fields still worked because the email check ran *earlier* in the matcher and claimed the field first. Nothing documented or tested that order. If someone reordered the checks, or a new label hit the broad pattern ("Address of previous employer"), behaviour would change silently. The guide calls the ordering "load-bearing". v0.2.0 tightens the location rule and adds tests that pin the precedence.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The regex was slow*: performance is not mentioned.
- *Email fields got the location value*: the guide says email fields filled correctly; the risk was latent.
- *Location ignored "city"*: "city" is in the pattern.

excerpts.quote: Today the email check at line 115 runs first and shields it, so the order of checks is load-bearing but nothing documents that.
Pinned by the "Email address", "bare 'Address'", "mailing address" and "employer address" tests in `fieldMatchers.test.ts`.

items.title: A rollback entry for an untouched select fired fake change events
items.body:
**Key: it fired change events on an untouched select and inflated the Cleared count.**

In v0.1.0 the rollback snapshot was pushed *before* `selectOption` ran, whether or not an option matched. When nothing matched, the select was not changed, but its entry stayed in the rollback list. "Clear values filled here" then wrote the same value back and dispatched `input`/`change` events on a field the extension never touched, and counted it as cleared. On wizard-style pages those events can mark untouched fields as edited. v0.2.0 pushes the entry only after a match.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Nothing visible*: rollback rewrote the select and fired events.
- *It threw*: the snapshot did store the previous value.
- *It erased the user's selection*: the value written back was the select's own unchanged value.

excerpts.quote: "Clear values filled here" then rewrites the select's unchanged value, dispatches `input`/`change` on a field the extension never modified, and inflates the "Cleared N" count.
const entry = snapshot(mapping.fieldId, element); const matched = selectOption(element, mapping.value); if (matched) { rollback.push(entry);

items.title: 'java' matched inside 'JavaScript' with high confidence
items.body:
**Key: 8, with high confidence.**

v0.1.0 matched skills with `text.includes(normalizedSkill)`. The question text contains "javascript", and "java" is a substring of it, so the check passed and the matcher returned `high("yearsOfExperience", "8", ...)`. That is the worst kind of error for this extension: wrong data, labelled "high", so it is written without review. v0.2.0 uses a whole-word regex and prefers the longest matching skill.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Nothing*: the substring check did match.
- *8 with medium confidence* (either wording): the old code returned `high(...)`, which is why the guide calls it precisely the category the extension promises to fill only when certain.

excerpts.quote: if (normalizedSkill && text.includes(normalizedSkill)) { return high("yearsOfExperience", String(years), ...); }
so it fills **8** with *high* confidence — precisely the category the extension promises to fill only when certain.

items.title: Validate the profile when it is saved, not when it is used
items.body:
**Key: the user sees the error while editing, not days later on a live job application.**

In v0.1.0 the bad entry was accepted on save. The crash came later, when `formatDate` read `date.month` on `undefined` in the middle of a real application, aborting the whole fill. Two fixes were possible: check entries when saving, or make `formatDate` tolerate bad data. The guide prefers save-time validation because the error appears where the user can fix it, in the options page, instead of on an application page days later.

Why the others are wrong:
- *A defensive formatDate is slower*: speed is not the reason given.
- *formatDate cannot change*: the guide lists a defensive `formatDate` as a valid alternative.
- *It also checks date order*: the Status line says date *order* is still not checked.

excerpts.quote: Validating at save time is better — it gives the user the error while they're editing, not days later on a live application page.
Date *order* (start before end) is not checked.

items.title: A data attribute on page controls reveals the extension
items.body:
**Key: page scripts and analytics can read it, revealing that the extension is installed.**

The scanner marks each control by writing `data-eli-apply-mate-field-id` into the page's own HTML. Those attributes stay there. The website's JavaScript, and any analytics tool that records the page's structure, can see them, and they are unique to this extension. That gives sites a "fingerprint": a way to detect that a visitor uses it. The suggested fix keeps the element-to-id map in a `WeakMap` inside the content script, invisible to the page. In v0.2.0 the finding is still open.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Attribute size limits*: the ids are short; no such limit is mentioned.
- *Breaks React and crashes the page*: the guide reports no crash; it calls this hygiene plus fingerprinting.
- *Duplicate ids block submission*: data attributes do not affect form submission.

excerpts.quote: and the attributes remain in the page DOM indefinitely (visible to the site's own JS and to any analytics that serialize the DOM — a fingerprintable marker that this extension is installed).
**Fix:** store a WeakMap from element → id inside the content script instead of writing DOM attributes

items.title: shouldFill is the safety boundary
items.body:
**Key: it moves the safety boundary, so unclear mappings get written instead of reviewed.**

`shouldFill` is one line: `return confidence === "high"`. In the autofill loop, any mapping for which it returns false goes to `unsure` and is shown for review; only the rest reach `fillField`. If it also returned true for "medium", every medium mapping (bare text yes/no questions, uncertain matches) would be written into the page. That turns "fill only when certain" into guessing, which is why tests should prove that medium stays review-only.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Only fields with no options*: medium covers more than that, and those fields are not skipped.
- *selectOption re-checks confidence*: `selectOption` only looks for a matching option.
- *Only the sidebar colours*: `shouldFill` decides what is written.

excerpts.quote: export function shouldFill(confidence: Confidence): boolean { return confidence === "high"; }
if (!shouldFill(mapping.confidence)) { unsure.push(mapping); continue; } const didFill = fillField(mapping, field, rollbackEntries);

items.title: The debug export copied what users had typed, unmasked
items.body:
**Key: it copied every field's valueBefore (whatever the user had typed) unmasked.**

The sidebar masks email and phone only in what it *shows*. "Copy debug JSON" serialized `result.detected`, and every detected field carries `valueBefore`: the value already in that control before the extension did anything. That could be a salary expectation or an ID number the user had typed, copied to the clipboard in plain text. v0.2.0 replaces every non-empty `valueBefore` with "[redacted]".

Why the others are wrong:
- *The full saved profile*: the export is the detected page fields, not the profile.
- *Uploaded to a remote endpoint*: the extension makes no network calls; it copies to the clipboard.
- *Masked values that can be reversed*: the problem was that `valueBefore` was not masked at all.

excerpts.quote: the "Copy debug JSON" button serializes `result.detected`, which includes `valueBefore` for every visible control on the page — anything the user already typed

// Never export what the user already typed on the page — mask valueBefore. const redacted = result.detected.map((field) => ({ ...field, valueBefore: field.valueBefore ? "[redacted]" : field.valueBefore }));

items.title: Unnamed radios in the same fieldset still merge
items.body:
**Key: no: the structural key applies only outside a fieldset.**

Read line 88 carefully: `input.name || fieldset ? "" : getStructuralKey(input)`. The `||` is evaluated first, so it means "if the input has a name *or* sits in a fieldset, use an empty structural key". Two unnamed questions inside one fieldset share the same type, empty name, same legend text and same form id, and both get `""` as structural key. Their group keys are identical, so they are still treated as one group. That is why the finding is only "Mostly fixed".

Why the others are wrong:
- *Because they lack a form id*: the form id is the same for both either way; the fieldset is what matters.
- *The legend differs per question*: one fieldset has one legend.
- *Every unnamed input gets a container key*: only those outside a fieldset do.

excerpts.quote: const structuralKey = input.name || fieldset ? "" : getStructuralKey(input); return [input.type, input.name, fieldsetText, input.form?.id, structuralKey].join("|");
Unnamed inputs inside the *same* fieldset still share one key, because the structural key is only used when there is no fieldset (`scanner.ts:88`).
